title: Interop & migration
scopeHtml: Scope: ComposeView in Views and Fragments, AndroidView and AndroidViewBinding in Compose, WebView/Map/Video hosting, theme and navigation interop, incremental migration strategy, and state and performance at the View/Compose boundary.

questions.promptHtml: How do you add Compose UI to an existing View-based screen, and what actually happens when you call setContent on a ComposeView?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand that Compose is hosted inside a normal View, not a parallel world, which explains every interop quirk later.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I put a ComposeView in the XML or create it in code, then call setContent { } with composables. ComposeView is an ordinary View. On attach it finds the ViewTreeLifecycleOwner, SavedStateRegistryOwner and ViewModelStoreOwner and creates a Composition tied to the window. For an Activity that is already ComponentActivity, setContent does the same thing for you.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ComposeView extends AbstractComposeView. Nothing composes until the view is attached to a window. At attach time it creates a Recomposer for the window (if none exists) and a Composition whose content is your lambda. It reads its owners through ViewTree*Owner.get(view). If none is set on the tree, it throws IllegalStateException: ViewTreeLifecycleOwner not found, which is the usual crash when you use it in a custom Dialog, PopupWindow or a plain Service window.

Activity/Fragment (owners) -> ViewTree*Owner set on decor/fragment view
   |
ComposeView (a View) --attach--> Recomposer + Composition(content lambda)
   |
AndroidComposeView (internal) -> layout / draw / input

Sizing follows normal View rules: wrap_content measures the composable content, match_parent fills the parent. Because it is a View, it participates in the parent's measure pass, so a parent that measures children multiple times (e.g. nested weights) makes Compose measure multiple times too (Compose supports this, but intrinsic measurement is still not free).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Activity that is already Compose-only
class ExampleActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent { MaterialTheme { Greeting("compose") } }
    }
}

// Existing View screen
val composeView = findViewById<ComposeView>(R.id.compose_view)
composeView.setContent { MaterialTheme { Greeting("compose") } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using ComposeView in a window without a ViewTreeLifecycleOwner (custom dialogs): crash on attach.
  • Forgetting activity-compose dependency when calling ComponentActivity.setContent.
  • Assuming content composes at setContent time; it composes on attach.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Compose get its lifecycle? → From ViewTreeLifecycleOwner on the view tree; Activities and Fragment views set it.
  2. Can I preview a ComposeView in the layout editor? → Yes, tools:composableName with the fully qualified name of a @Preview composable.
  3. What if two ComposeViews are in one layout? → Each needs a unique id or their saved state keys collide.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "call setContent". Senior: explains attach-time composition, the owner lookup, why dialogs crash, and the unique-ID rule for state restore.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved a bottom sheet into a custom Dialog hosting a ComposeView and crashed on attach until they set the three ViewTree owners on the dialog window's decor view.

questions.promptHtml: What is ViewCompositionStrategy, what is the default, and which strategies exist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the single most common source of state-loss and leak bugs in hybrid apps; interviewers want to see you know the disposal model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It decides when a ComposeView disposes its Composition, which cancels effects and drops remember state. The default is DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool: dispose on window detach, except inside pooling containers like RecyclerView where it waits until the pool container detaches or the item is discarded. In Fragments I use DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy Disposes when Use for
DisposeOnDetachedFromWindow View detaches Superseded by the OrReleasedFromPool variant
DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool (default) Detach, or pool release/discard Standalone ComposeView; RecyclerView items
DisposeOnLifecycleDestroyed(lifecycle) The given Lifecycle is DESTROYED Lifecycle known up front
DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed The ViewTreeLifecycleOwner found at attach is DESTROYED Fragment views; lifecycle not known yet

The default is right for a Compose-only app. In a mixed app a view can detach and reattach without its owner being destroyed (Fragment on the back stack, ViewPager2 page, ViewGroup.removeView then re-add). With the default, each detach tears down the composition: remember state is lost, LaunchedEffects are cancelled, and rememberSaveable is the only survivor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
composeView.setViewCompositionStrategy(
    ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving the default in a Fragment: the fragment view lifecycle outlives the detach on the back stack; state resets.
  • Setting the strategy after setContent has attached; set it before attach.
  • Using DisposeOnLifecycleDestroyed(activity.lifecycle) for a Fragment view: leaks the composition (and the view) until the Activity dies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always use the Fragment lifecycle? → Inside RecyclerView you want disposal on pool release, not on the host lifecycle.
  2. What does disposal actually do? → Runs onDispose, cancels the effect coroutine scope, forgets remembered objects (RememberObserver.onForgotten).
  3. How does rememberSaveable fare? → Survives via the SavedStateRegistry as long as the ComposeView has a stable id and the owner restores.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names the options. Senior: ties each to which lifecycle owns the view, and can predict which state survives a back-stack round trip.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout form lost half-typed input after the user opened and closed a help screen, because the host Fragment's view detached and the default strategy disposed remember state.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the correct way to host a ComposeView in a Fragment, including binding cleanup and saved state.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most real migrations go through Fragments; leaks and lost state here are routine.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Create or inflate the ComposeView in onCreateView, set DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed before setContent, give it a stable id if there are multiple, and null any ViewBinding in onDestroyView. Collect ViewModel state with collectAsStateWithLifecycle inside the composable so it follows the Fragment's view lifecycle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Fragment has two lifecycles: the Fragment and its view (viewLifecycleOwner). The Fragment's view is destroyed and recreated on back-stack navigation while the Fragment instance lives. DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed resolves the owner from the view tree at attach, which for a Fragment's view is viewLifecycleOwner, so the composition dies exactly when the view does. Using the Fragment's own lifecycle would leak the composition across onDestroyView.

Saved state: each ComposeView saves rememberSaveable data under its view id. Two ComposeViews with no/duplicate ids overwrite each other's saved state (the docs state unique IDs are required for savedInstanceState; ids declared in res/values/ids.xml).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedFragment : Fragment() {
    private val vm: FeedViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater, container: ViewGroup?, state: Bundle?
    ): View = ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
        setViewCompositionStrategy(
            ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed
        )
        setContent {
            val ui by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
            FeedScreen(ui, onRetry = vm::retry)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Capturing binding or this@Fragment in the composable and outliving the view.
  • Collecting with collectAsState (not lifecycle-aware) so flows keep running while the Fragment view is STOPPED.
  • Using Fragment by viewModels() with ids but holding UI state in the Fragment instead of the ViewModel.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. viewModels() or activityViewModels() for shared state? → Scope to the narrowest owner that survives; shared across fragments only when truly shared.
  2. What about AndroidFragment? → That is the reverse direction (Fragment inside Compose).
  3. How do you test it? → createAndroidComposeRule plus FragmentScenario, or Espresso with onView for the host plus onNodeWithTag for compose parts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: sets content in onCreateView. Senior: talks about view lifecycle vs fragment lifecycle, binding nulling, ids, and lifecycle-aware collection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leak report showed Fragment views retained after navigation; the cause was a ComposeView with the Activity lifecycle as disposal owner.

questions.promptHtml: Explain AndroidView: what do factory and update do, when does each run, and what are the classic pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests your mental model of Compose-to-View data flow, and the most common interop bug is misusing update.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: factory runs once per composition-node to create the View; update runs right after creation and again whenever a snapshot State read inside it changes or the lambda is recomposed with changed inputs. So factory is for one-time setup and listeners, update is for pushing the latest state into the View, and it must be cheap and idempotent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AndroidView wraps the View in a layout node (AndroidViewHolder). update is observed in a snapshot: State read inside it invalidates only that block, not the whole parent. Docs say the Composable "recomposes whenever a State read within the callback changes".

composition enters -> factory(context) -> View created, attached
                   -> update(view)      (observed)
state read in update changes -> update(view) again (no re-create)
composition leaves -> onRelease(view)

The rule: never put the View in remember outside AndroidView; the docs recommend creating it in factory. Pitfalls: (1) side-effecting work in update (e.g. loadUrl) runs on every change; (2) listeners captured in factory hold the first lambda, so a changed callback silently goes stale unless you re-assign it in update or use rememberUpdatedState; (3) heavy views created each time because keys changed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Chart(data: List<Point>, onPointClick: (Point) -> Unit) {
    val currentClick by rememberUpdatedState(onPointClick)
    AndroidView(
        factory = { ctx -> ChartView(ctx).apply { setOnPointClick { currentClick(it) } } },
        update = { view -> if (view.data !== data) view.data = data }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling view.setText(...) unconditionally, causing cursor jumps or relayout loops.
  • Capturing stale lambdas in factory listeners.
  • Expecting update to be called only once.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not hold the View in remember? → Lifecycle of the View then diverges from the layout node; docs recommend factory.
  2. How do you reach the View from outside? → Capture a reference in factory into a state holder, or expose an imperative controller object.
  3. Does the View recompose? → No; Views do not recompose, only your update lambda re-executes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "factory creates, update updates". Senior: names idempotency, stale-listener capture and where the View's lifetime really ends.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chart wrapper re-assigned a 5k-point dataset in update on every parent recomposition (tooltip state change), costing ~12 ms per frame until guarded by identity checks.

questions.contextHtml:
A hybrid app embeds a help article via AndroidView(WebView). Since the Compose migration, QA reports: the page reloads and scrolls to top whenever the user toggles a bookmark icon in the same screen; 3% of sessions show a blank white WebView after returning from background; Firebase shows rising memory (+80 MB over 15 screens). Code:

@Composable
fun ArticleScreen(url: String, bookmarked: Boolean, onToggle: () -> Unit) {
    Column {
        IconButton(onClick = onToggle) { Icon(bookmarkIcon(bookmarked), null) }
        AndroidView(
            factory = { ctx -> WebView(ctx).apply { settings.javaScriptEnabled = true } },
            update = { webView ->
                webView.webViewClient = WebViewClient()
                webView.loadUrl(url)
            }
        )
    }
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in remember" or "use a ViewModel". It misses that update re-executes and that nothing destroys the WebView.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are urls ever changing in-place? Do we need to keep scroll/back-forward history across process death? Is JS content authenticated (cookies)? Which min API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Guard loadUrl so it only runs when the url changed; ship as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) update unconditionally calls loadUrl and re-sets the client: reload on any recomposition (toggle recomposes parent, passes same url, update re-runs because the lambda changed). (b) No onRelease to destroy() the WebView: memory growth, native renderer retained. (c) No lifecycle forwarding (onPause/onResume) and no state save: blank view after background. Red herring: JavaScript being enabled.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in update to count calls; Android Studio memory profiler heap dump filtering WebView; LeakCanary; chrome://inspect for renderer state.
  5. Root cause: update is not "on url change", it is "whenever the lambda re-executes with changed captures or observed state changes". Reassigning the client and reloading each time resets the page. Without onRelease, WebView (holding a Context and a renderer) is only collected when GC runs.
  6. Fix:
AndroidView(
    factory = { ctx ->
        WebView(ctx).apply {
            settings.javaScriptEnabled = true
            webViewClient = WebViewClient()
            tag = null
        }
    },
    update = { wv -> if (wv.tag != url) { wv.tag = url; wv.loadUrl(url) } },
    onRelease = { wv -> wv.stopLoading(); wv.destroy() }
)

Long-term: a WebView state holder that survives rotation (saveState/restoreState bundle through rememberSaveable or ViewModel) and forward lifecycle events (LifecycleEventObserver calling onPause/onResume). Google's current guidance wraps WebView through AndroidView too; verify whether the official androidx.webkit Compose helpers exist for your version before depending on a third-party. 7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no network or navigation side effects in update without a guard; leak test with LeakCanary in a UI test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keep a global WebView singleton (cookie and theme bleed). Not remember { WebView(context) } outside AndroidView (its lifecycle is no longer tied to the node).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Back navigation inside the WebView? → BackHandler(enabled = wv.canGoBack()) calling goBack().
  • Same WebView across tabs? → Keep per-tab state holders; pooling needs onReset; but never share across contexts.
  • Tests? → Robolectric lacks real WebView; use instrumented tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A news app saw 40% more renderer OOM kills after migration; every article screen leaked a WebView since nobody called destroy. A 6-line onRelease cut it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Compose, suggests remember.
  • Hire: guards update, adds onRelease.
  • Strong hire: also state save/restore, lifecycle forwarding, back handling and a leak test.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when you put an AndroidView inside a LazyColumn item, and how do onReset and onRelease change that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know the cost of View inflation in lazy lists and the reuse overload.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: By default, when an item scrolls out of composition its View is discarded, and a new item's factory runs again, so you pay inflation per item. The overload with onReset (non-null) lets Compose pool and reuse the View: onReset is called to clean it for reuse, update follows, and onRelease fires only when the View leaves composition permanently.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy lists reuse compositions by content type (reuseComposition). With the plain AndroidView overload, the View is not reusable. With the overload added in 1.4.0-rc01 per the docs, onReset marks the View as reusable. The docs note onReset may not be immediately followed by update (verify per version), so onReset must clear listeners, text, scroll position and in-flight work.

Pair with contentType on the items call so a reuse never swaps unrelated View types.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    items(rows, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "ad" }) { row ->
        AndroidView(
            factory = { AdView(it) },
            update = { it.bind(row) },
            onReset = { it.clear() },
            onRelease = { it.destroy() }
        )
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Omitting onReset: no reuse, repeated inflation.
  • Not clearing state in onReset: previous row's content flashes.
  • Missing contentType.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not RecyclerView with ComposeView items instead? → Valid if the list is still View-based; use the default pool-aware strategy.
  2. Where do you cancel image loads? → onReset.
  3. Memory impact? → Pooled Views stay alive until released; cap the pool by content types.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it works in LazyColumn". Senior: knows reuse needs onReset, contentType, and that update isn't guaranteed to follow.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed with ad Views inflated 8 per screen scroll hit 11% jank until onReset-based reuse was added.

questions.promptHtml: How do you embed an XML layout or an existing Fragment inside Compose, and why is that considered transitional?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps have legacy screens that are too risky to rewrite; you must have the bridge tools in hand.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For XML I use AndroidViewBinding(MyBinding::inflate) { ... } from androidx.compose.ui:ui-viewbinding with view binding enabled. For a Fragment I use the AndroidFragment<T>() composable from androidx.fragment:fragment-compose. Both are for the transition, since a Compose-only app should not need Fragments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AndroidViewBinding inflates the binding once, and the block runs on inflate and on changes to State read within, same semantics as update. AndroidFragment manages adding and removing the Fragment as the composable enters/leaves the composition and exposes arguments, fragmentState and onUpdate. With Fragment 1.9.0+ you can cap maxLifecycle, e.g. keep off-screen pager pages at STARTED and only the settled page at RESUMED.

Fragment-in-Compose has cost: a Fragment manager transaction, a second lifecycle, and the "Fragment id" of the host container. State restore uses the Fragment saved state, not rememberSaveable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun LegacyPromo() {
    AndroidViewBinding(PromoBinding::inflate) {
        title.text = "Spring sale"
    }
}

@Composable
fun LegacyScreen() {
    AndroidFragment<OldCheckoutFragment>(arguments = bundleOf("id" to 7))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using AndroidViewBinding for a full screen in a Compose-only app (docs advise small legacy layouts only).
  • Writing to binding views outside the block.
  • Using the Fragment inside a Lazy item and expecting cheap reuse.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fragment version needed? → fragment-compose artifact; maxLifecycle needs Fragment 1.9.0+ per the docs; verify the exact artifact version.
  2. How do Fragment results reach Compose? → setFragmentResultListener or shared ViewModel via onUpdate.
  3. Why transitional? → Two lifecycles, extra memory, and Navigation Compose cannot host it natively.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names the composable. Senior: explains lifecycle capping and why you plan their removal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payments flow Fragment wrapped via AndroidFragment let the team ship a Compose home screen first and delay the risky rewrite by two quarters.

questions.promptHtml: Your app has an XML Material theme and new Compose screens. How do you keep the look consistent across both?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Visual drift between View and Compose screens is the first thing designers notice in a hybrid app.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compose does not read your XML theme automatically. MaterialTheme in Compose is separate from the Theme.* in styles.xml. I either map values by hand into a Compose theme, or use an adapter library, or best, define the tokens once (colors, type, shapes) and generate both. Long term, the Compose theme is the source of truth.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two theme systems coexist: the View theme (resolved through ?attr/ and ContextThemeWrapper) and Compose's MaterialTheme (CompositionLocals for ColorScheme, Typography, Shapes). The Accompanist themeadapter-material/material3 libraries read XML attributes into Compose themes but are deprecated/archived (verify current status before choosing). The reverse direction matters too: a ComposeView inside a View screen inherits nothing, and an AndroidView inside Compose gets the host Context's theme, so a View theme overlay (ContextThemeWrapper) must be applied if it needs a different one.

Dark theme and dynamic color must be handled in both: isSystemInDarkTheme() for Compose vs uiMode night qualifier resources for Views; they agree when following system, but an in-app toggle must update both (AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode recreates Activities; Compose follows via configuration).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun AppTheme(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    val dark = isSystemInDarkTheme()
    MaterialTheme(
        colorScheme = if (dark) DarkColors else LightColors, // mirror colors.xml tokens
        typography = AppTypography,
        content = content
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hex duplication in two places, drifting after a rebrand.
  • Wrapping each ComposeView in different theme variants.
  • Forgetting the ripple/shape/textAppearance differences (M2 vs M3 mixes).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. M2 XML with M3 Compose? → Visible differences in elevation tint and shape; migrate tokens deliberately.
  2. In-app dark toggle? → Drive both from one preference; recreate on change.
  3. Automate sync? → Generate colors.xml and Color.kt from a design-token JSON in the build.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: copy colors. Senior: single token source, adapters' maintenance risk, night-mode toggle behavior.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a rebrand, three Compose screens kept the old primary color since only colors.xml was updated; a token generator ended recurrence.

questions.promptHtml: How do you keep state consistent when the same data is read and written by both a View (say an EditText) and a composable? What breaks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Two-way sync loops and dual sources of truth are where hybrid screens get subtle bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One source of truth, owned outside both: a ViewModel StateFlow or a Compose state holder. Compose reads it and pushes to the View in update; the View reports events upward via listeners. I guard against echo loops by comparing before writing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The View side is imperative and mutable, the Compose side is declarative. Data flows down (state to View through update), events flow up (listener to ViewModel). The classic bug is an EditText with a TextWatcher: user types, listener updates state, update calls setText, which triggers the TextWatcher again and moves the cursor or loops.

ViewModel.state --> Compose --> update{ if (view.text != s) setText(s) }
     ^                                       |
     +------ listener (user input) <---------+

Another failure: the View holds its own state (scroll offset, selection) that Compose does not know, so a recomposition resets it, or on onReset reuse it carries over. Save View state explicitly if it matters (saveHierarchyState is automatic only for Views with ids inside a saved host; AndroidView inside Compose gets restoration through its own registry; verify for your version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
AndroidView(
    factory = { ctx -> EditText(ctx).apply {
        doAfterTextChanged { onTextChange(it.toString()) }
    } },
    update = { et -> if (et.text.toString() != text) et.setText(text) }
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing setText unconditionally; cursor jumps to start.
  • Keeping a copy of state in both View and ViewModel.
  • Doing async transforms between View event and state so the View shows stale text.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use TextField? → That is the right answer if possible; an EditText is for IME features not yet in Compose or legacy.
  2. How to avoid recursion? → Equality guard plus a suppress flag if the equality check is lossy.
  3. How does it affect process death? → The ViewModel owns the truth; use SavedStateHandle for restorable parts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "pass state down, callbacks up". Senior: identifies echo loops, View-owned state (scroll, selection), and chooses a single owner.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legacy rich-text editor wrapped in AndroidView jumped the cursor to position 0 on every keystroke once the ViewModel round-trip became async.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app: 120 screens, 70 Fragments, XML + RxJava, 3 Android squads (14 devs), crash-free rate 99.6%, monthly releases, 2.1M DAU. Leadership wants "full Compose in 12 months" and the CTO fears regressions in the KYC and payments flows (together ~35% of revenue). APK size 48 MB, cold start p50 1.4 s. A past rewrite attempt was abandoned.
questions.promptHtml: Propose the migration plan and how you would defend it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite everything screen by screen starting with the home screen", with no ordering by risk, no measurement, no stop criteria.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have UI tests and screenshot tests today? Is there a design system or is it ad hoc? Which flows churn most (change frequency drives ROI)? What is the Compose skill level per squad? Is the Navigation component Fragment-based?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (planning). First two weeks: set the baseline (startup, jank, APK, crash-free) with Macrobenchmark so we can prove no regression, and enable Compose in one low-risk module.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) Perf regressions on cold start from the Compose runtime and first-frame init. (b) Hybrid screens with two lifecycles and state loss. (c) Navigation rewrite blocking everything. (d) Skill spread: inconsistent patterns. (e) APK/method count growth.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark startup and scroll before/after; baseline profiles; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; compiler metrics; LeakCanary; size diff in CI.
  5. Root cause (of why rewrites fail): Big-bang rewrites combine UI, architecture and navigation changes with no measurable intermediate state.
  6. Fix (the plan): Phase 0 shared design system module in Compose. Phase 1 all new screens in Compose inside Fragments via ComposeView. Phase 2 migrate low-risk, high-churn screens (settings, lists) bottom-up. Phase 3 leaf-up replacement inside mixed screens. Phase 4 after the last Fragment goes, move to Navigation Compose. KYC/payments last, behind feature flags and screenshot tests, with parity checks.
  7. Prevention: Per-phase exit criteria and budgets (startup +30 ms max, jank not worse), lint banning new XML, screenshot tests as the safety net, a migration dashboard counting screens.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not promise 12 months full; I'd commit to a measured percent and renegotiate. Not migrate payments first, not rewrite navigation and UI in the same release, not drop Rx or MVVM at the same time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Perf regression found in Phase 2? → Stop the line, fix with baseline profile and recomposition work before more screens.
  • A squad refuses? → Pair migration, templates, and a component library lowers entry cost.
  • Can we skip hybrid? → Not for 70 Fragments; hybrid is the plan, not the compromise.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team mandated "no new XML" and shipped a design-system module first; the next 40 screens landed at half the earlier cost, while the payment flow stayed XML for a year behind tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang or arbitrary order.
  • Hire: bottom-up, new-screens-first, measuring.
  • Strong hire: risk-ordered, exit criteria, perf baselines, navigation sequencing, honest timeline.

questions.promptHtml: You have a Fragment-based Navigation component graph and are adding Compose screens. How do you handle navigation during migration, and when can you adopt Navigation Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Navigation is where hybrid migrations stall; sequencing it wrong causes rewrites.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep Fragment navigation while any destination is a Fragment. Each new Compose screen is a Fragment hosting a ComposeView, with the same nav graph, safe args and back stack. Only when every destination is a composable do I move to Navigation Compose; mixed content within a screen is fine.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official guidance, all navigation destinations must be composables before Navigation Compose migration; screen-level composables can still contain Views. Until then the Fragment NavController owns the back stack. A common bridge: each Fragment hosts a Compose screen and takes a NavController callback via the screen's parameters (not passing NavController into deep composables).

Option for the end game: a Compose NavHost can sit inside a Fragment as one destination, giving a nested Compose graph while the outer graph remains Fragment-based; it works but has two back-stack systems, so back handling must be unified with OnBackPressedCallback/BackHandler carefully. Navigation 3 is the newer recommended direction in the docs for Compose-only apps (verify stability for your target).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DetailFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreateView(i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle?) =
        ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
            setViewCompositionStrategy(
                ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
            setContent {
                DetailScreen(onOpenItem = { id ->
                    findNavController().navigate(DetailFragmentDirections.toItem(id))
                })
            }
        }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing NavController through the composable tree (untestable, breaks previews).
  • Two back stacks fighting for back press.
  • Deep links defined in both graphs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Shared ViewModel between destinations? → hiltNavGraphViewModel/navGraphViewModels on the Fragment side; mapped to nav backstack entries on Compose side.
  2. Shared element transitions? → Differ between systems; plan per flow.
  3. Result passing? → Fragment results API during hybrid; SavedStateHandle on back stack entries after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use NavHost". Senior: sequencing, single owner of back stack, screen-level callbacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team nested a Compose NavHost inside a Fragment and shipped double-back handling that exited the app from the second screen; a single back dispatcher fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app (800k DAU) moved its Product Detail screen into a ViewPager2 whose pages are Fragments with ComposeView content, default strategy. After release 5.12: crash-free users 99.4% to 99.1%; support reports "form I filled in disappears when I swipe back to page 1"; Crashlytics shows IllegalStateException: Disposed composition rare (0.2%). QA cannot reproduce on emulators; reproduces on low-RAM devices (3 GB) after opening the camera.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use rememberSaveable everywhere" without understanding why the composition is disposed, or "disable offscreen limit".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is offscreenPageLimit set? Does the page Fragment's view get destroyed? What changed in 5.12 (library bump, Fragment version)? Are effects launched in the composition touching the disposed scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the fix behind a flag; set the right strategy and ship a hotfix; hold the rollout at 20% until crash-free recovers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Default DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool disposes when ViewPager2 detaches the page's view, wiping remember state. (b) A callback (camera result or coroutine) completing after disposal touches released state: the rare crash. (c) Low-memory process death restoring without stable ids. Red herring: emulator memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log DisposableEffect.onDispose in the form; Layout Inspector with page swipes; developer option "Don't keep activities"; adb am kill for process death; check ComposeView ids.
  5. Root cause: Detach is not destroy. ViewPager2 detaches pages that remain Fragment-alive; default strategy disposes on detach so unsaved state disappears, and stale async work resumed into a disposed composition.
  6. Fix: Short term: DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed and move the form state into a ViewModel (scoped to the Fragment) or rememberSaveable. Long term: hoist all form state to a state holder; use collectAsStateWithLifecycle; launch async work from the ViewModel scope, not from composition.
  7. Prevention: Instrumented test that swipes away and back asserting field text; "Don't keep activities" job on CI; lint review check for strategy on every ComposeView in a Fragment.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keep all pages resumed (battery/CPU); not rely on rememberSaveable alone for large objects (Bundle size limits).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only on low RAM? → Fragment view destroyed and recreated by the system; same root cause.
  • Replace ViewPager2 with HorizontalPager? → Possible, but a bigger change; state hoisting is required anyway.
  • Can the strategy be set globally? → No global switch; wrap in a helper factory.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A form with 11 fields lost data on 4% of swipes; the fix was two lines plus one ViewModel move, but finding it took a week because emulators had spare RAM.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random mitigations.
  • Hire: identifies strategy and hoists state.
  • Strong hire: also async work after disposal, test for it, process-death coverage.

questions.promptHtml: How do you host a MapView, PlayerView (ExoPlayer/Media3) or WebView in Compose correctly? What lifecycle work is on you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These Views have their own lifecycle callbacks that Compose will not call for you; skipping them leaks or crashes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I create the View in factory, push state in update, and forward the host lifecycle to it with a LifecycleEventObserver registered in a DisposableEffect, because MapView needs onCreate/onStart/onResume/onPause/onStop/onDestroy and WebView needs onPause/onResume/destroy. For video I own the Player in a state holder, attach it to PlayerView in update and release it independently in onRelease/ViewModel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AndroidView only handles creation, update and removal. The View's own lifecycle contract is not tied to Compose. A MapView (Google Maps SDK) requires explicit lifecycle forwarding; the Maps Compose library does this for you, which is the preferred option if available. For PlayerView, the player outlives the view: configuration change or scroll should not rebuild the player; keep it in a ViewModel or remember with a release in onDispose.

SurfaceView-based views (video, maps) can draw above Compose content or flicker during animations or scrolling in lazy lists; test z-ordering. TextureView-based players integrate better with transforms and clipping at the cost of memory/battery.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun rememberMapViewWithLifecycle(): MapView {
    val context = LocalContext.current
    val mapView = remember { MapView(context) }
    val lifecycle = LocalLifecycleOwner.current.lifecycle
    DisposableEffect(lifecycle, mapView) {
        val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, e ->
            when (e) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE -> mapView.onCreate(Bundle())
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_START -> mapView.onStart()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME -> mapView.onResume()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_PAUSE -> mapView.onPause()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_STOP -> mapView.onStop()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY -> mapView.onDestroy()
                else -> {}
            }
        }
        lifecycle.addObserver(observer)
        onDispose { lifecycle.removeObserver(observer); mapView.onDestroy() }
    }
    return mapView
}

(Note: remembering the View outside AndroidView deviates from the docs' advice for ordinary Views; Maps docs historically use this pattern. Prefer Maps Compose; verify.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never forwarding onPause, so playback or location updates continue in background.
  • Creating the player inside factory so it dies on every scroll out.
  • Calling onDestroy twice.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a state holder for the player? → Survives configuration change and list scroll; one owner of release.
  2. Z-order glitches? → SurfaceView composited separately; use TextureView or avoid overlaying.
  3. Picture-in-picture? → Activity-level concern; the PlayerView needs to be re-attached to the same player.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: wraps the View. Senior: forwards lifecycle, separates the player lifetime from the View, thinks about surface type.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background-playing video kept decoding after navigation because onPause was never forwarded; battery complaints followed.

questions.contextHtml: A social feed (RecyclerView, 1.5M DAU, 50% devices with 3-4 GB RAM) replaced its post card with a ComposeView item. Result: p95 frame time 31 ms to 52 ms while scrolling, jank rate 6% to 19%, onCreateViewHolder takes ~14 ms per card (Perfetto), and fast-fling shows blank cards for ~150 ms. Cards contain image, 3 text styles, a reaction row. Team says "Compose is slow".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert to XML" or "add remember everywhere".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Release build with R8 and baseline profile? One ComposeView per item or a nested ComposeView? What strategy is used? setHasFixedSize, recycledViewPool sizing, any nested scroll?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn the flag off for the segment on lowest-RAM devices while we fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Debug or no baseline profile: Compose code interpreted at first use (huge in onCreateViewHolder). (b) Wrong or custom strategy re-creating compositions on each bind. (c) Heavy item: unstable params causing recompose, no keys. (d) Item height unknown, causing re-measure. Red herring: image library.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric with and without baseline profiles; Perfetto trace sections Compose:recompose, Compose:measure; compiler reports for unstable classes; Layout Inspector recomposition counts.
  5. Root cause: First-use JIT costs plus ComposeView creation per ViewHolder (a new Composition, Recomposer wiring) and an unstable Post model making every rebind recompose all children.
  6. Fix: Ship baseline profiles (compose libraries ship profiles but the app's own composables need one); keep the default strategy, which is pool-aware (disposes when the pool releases the item); use setContent once in the ViewHolder constructor and push data through a MutableState in the holder; stabilize the model (immutable, or strong skipping where on); increase pool size for the item type.
class PostHolder(val composeView: ComposeView) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(composeView) {
    private var post by mutableStateOf<Post?>(null)
    init { composeView.setContent { post?.let { PostCard(it) } } }
    fun bind(p: Post) { post = p }
}
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test in CI with thresholds; compiler metrics report review.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not call setContent in onBindViewHolder (re-creates composition per bind); not keep both XML and Compose in parallel indefinitely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not migrate the whole list to LazyColumn? → Likely the end state; only after parity measured.
  • Items with different heights? → Provide contentType in Lazy; in RecyclerView use view types.
  • Still 40 ms after fixes? → Check overdraw, image decoding thread, and nested ComposeViews.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Baseline profile plus a stable model dropped p95 from 52 ms to 29 ms with no UI changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reverts.
  • Hire: baseline profile, setContent placement.
  • Strong hire: measures with Macrobenchmark and Perfetto, understands strategy and pooling.

questions.subtopic: Touch, insets, scroll at the boundary
questions.promptHtml: What goes wrong with touch handling, nested scrolling, window insets and sizing when Compose and Views are nested inside each other, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are the interop bugs that survive code review and appear only on-device.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Four categories. Scroll: a ComposeView inside a scrolling View parent can get unbounded height, and a vertical LazyColumn inside a ScrollView crashes with infinite constraints. Nested scroll: Compose and Views interoperate through the nested scroll protocol, but you must check each direction. Touch: AndroidView consumes events it handles, and parents may intercept. Insets: apply them once, not at both layers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sizing: ComposeView with wrap_content inside ScrollView measures with unbounded height; a lazy list then throws ("Vertically scrollable component was measured with an infinity maximum height constraints"). Fix by giving a bounded height or replacing the ScrollView with the Compose container.

Nested scroll: Compose's nestedScroll modifier interoperates with the View NestedScrollingParent3 system; Compose scrollables dispatch to View parents (e.g. CoordinatorLayout/AppBarLayout) and AndroidView participates as child. Edge cases around fling dispatch differ by version; test per release (verify).

Touch: Compose consumes pointer events in its own tree; a Compose item inside a View-based horizontal pager can fight swipe, needing requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent handling in the View child or using Compose's built-in handling.

Insets: enableEdgeToEdge and WindowInsets in Compose vs fitsSystemWindows/ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener. If both layers pad, you get double padding; if neither, content draws under bars. Pick one layer to consume and mark consumed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bounded height instead of a LazyColumn in an unbounded parent
AndroidView(factory = { ctx ->
    ComposeView(ctx).apply { setContent { Content() } }
}, modifier = Modifier.height(300.dp))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• LazyColumn in ScrollView / NestedScrollView.
  • Double inset padding; keyboard (IME) insets ignored in the View layer.
  • Assuming Compose gestures stop parent interception automatically.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fix for lazy in scroll parent? → Make one scroller own it; or fixed height.
  2. How do you debug touch? → Layout Inspector plus pointerInput logging; adb shell dumpsys input.
  3. Accessibility? → Compose semantics merge into the View accessibility tree; check TalkBack traversal order across the boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: knows the unbounded crash. Senior: also nested scroll, insets ownership, accessibility traversal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Edge-to-edge rollout doubled bottom padding on screens where both the Fragment root and the Compose Scaffold consumed navigation bar insets.

questions.contextHtml: Postmortem: release 7.3 (hybrid app, 1.1M DAU) saw OOM crashes rising from 0.15% to 0.9% sessions within 4 days, concentrated on 2 GB devices after 20+ minutes of use. Heap dumps show 61 retained instances of CheckoutFragment views, each holding a ComposeView, an AndroidView WebView, and an Activity context. LeakCanary (debug) had flagged it in two PRs earlier but was marked "known". Stack excerpt: GC root: ... kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope -> ComposeView -> CheckoutFragment.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: cause, fix, process changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A developer forgot to clean up", with no systemic fix.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What created the long-lived scope (singleton, application scope, GlobalScope)? Which strategy is on the ComposeView? Was WebView.destroy() ever called? Did the Fragment view binding get nulled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server flag to route Checkout to a lightweight path or disable the WebView promo; hotfix release; staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A long-lived coroutine/flow collector started in composition (via a captured application-scope) holding the composable's captured Fragment. (b) DisposeOnLifecycleDestroyed(activity) keeps composition alive. (c) WebView never destroyed. (d) Static callback registry holding a listener.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump path-to-GC-root in Studio profiler; LeakCanary traces; grep strategies; check onRelease.
  5. Root cause: A lambda inside setContent captured this@CheckoutFragment and was registered into an application-scope flow collector; the ComposeView used the Activity lifecycle for disposal, so neither disposal nor scope cancellation happened at onDestroyView.
  6. Fix: DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed; collect via collectAsStateWithLifecycle in composition, not from an app scope; onRelease destroying WebView; remove Fragment references from lambdas (pass the ViewModel).
  7. Prevention: LeakCanary failures block merges (no "known" bucket without a ticket); an instrumented leak test with LeakAssertions on the flow; code review checklist: strategy, scopes, onRelease; release-gate OOM monitoring with alert at 0.3%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not suppress with WeakReference hacks; not blame individuals; not delay the hotfix to add the process changes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why only 2 GB devices? → Lower heap limits, so the same leak crosses OOM sooner.
  • How would you have caught it earlier? → Soak test (navigate 50 times) with heap assertions.
  • Is it a Compose bug? → No; owner mis-binding and scope misuse.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Every retained view cost ~9 MB (WebView renderer plus bitmaps); 60 instances matched the observed 500 MB growth.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blame and patch.
  • Hire: finds strategy and scope, fixes both.
  • Strong hire: process changes, soak test, device-mix explanation with numbers.
